author: KERNAL Content Team
title: Unsupervised Learning & Clustering
subtitle: K-means, DBSCAN, PCA, and finding hidden structure

whyItExists.problem: Many datasets have no labels — you cannot know in advance how many natural groups exist or what they represent. You need to explore the data's hidden structure without a predefined target.
whyItExists.solution: Clustering algorithms automatically group similar data points together without labels. PCA reduces high-dimensional data to 2-3 dimensions for visualisation and noise removal.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Customer segmentation, anomaly detection, data exploration, compressing high-dimensional data before supervised learning, and discovering natural groups in biological or scientific data.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: When you have labels — supervised learning will always outperform clustering for classification tasks. Clustering is exploratory; don't use it when you have a defined prediction target.

explainModes.beginner: Clustering is like sorting a bag of mixed sweets into groups by colour and shape, without anyone telling you how many groups there should be. The algorithm figures out which sweets are most similar and groups them together.
explainModes.simple: K-means picks K starting points, assigns every data point to its nearest centre, then moves each centre to the average of its group. It repeats until centres stop moving. DBSCAN groups points that are densely packed together.
explainModes.standard: K-means minimises within-cluster sum of squares by iteratively assigning points to their nearest centroid and recomputing centroids. DBSCAN defines clusters as dense regions separated by low-density areas, naturally identifying outliers. PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance.
explainModes.technical: K-means solves a non-convex optimisation via Lloyd's algorithm — not guaranteed to find the global optimum. K-means++ initialisation improves stability. DBSCAN has time complexity O(n log n) with spatial indexing. PCA solves the eigenvalue decomposition of the covariance matrix.
explainModes.deepDive: K-means is equivalent to a Gaussian Mixture Model with equal, spherical covariances and hard assignment. GMMs use EM (Expectation-Maximisation) for soft assignment. UMAP and t-SNE are non-linear dimensionality reduction methods that preserve local structure better than PCA.

content.text: Unsupervised learning finds hidden structure in unlabelled data. There is no target variable — the algorithm discovers patterns on its own. The two most important techniques are clustering (grouping similar points) and dimensionality reduction (compressing high-dimensional data).

K-means partitions data into K clusters by minimising within-cluster variance. Each point belongs to the cluster with the nearest centroid. The algorithm iterates: assign → recompute centroids → reassign — until convergence.

content.code:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Always scale before clustering
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_sc = scaler.fit_transform(X)

# Fit K-means
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=4, init='k-means++', n_init=10, random_state=42)
labels = kmeans.fit_predict(X_sc)

print(f'Inertia (within-cluster SS): {kmeans.inertia_:.2f}')
print(f'Silhouette score: {silhouette_score(X_sc, labels):.3f}')  # -1 to 1, higher is better
print(f'Cluster sizes: {np.bincount(labels)}')

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

inertias = []
silhouettes = []
K_range = range(2, 12)

for k in K_range:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, init='k-means++', n_init=10, random_state=42)
    labels = km.fit_predict(X_sc)
    inertias.append(km.inertia_)
    silhouettes.append(silhouette_score(X_sc, labels))

# Plot elbow — look for the 'kink'
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
ax1.plot(K_range, inertias, 'bx-')
ax1.set_xlabel('K')
ax1.set_ylabel('Inertia')
ax1.set_title('Elbow Method')

ax2.plot(K_range, silhouettes, 'rx-')
ax2.set_xlabel('K')
ax2.set_ylabel('Silhouette Score')
ax2.set_title('Silhouette Analysis')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

best_k = K_range[np.argmax(silhouettes)]
print(f'Best K by silhouette: {best_k}')

content.text: DBSCAN finds clusters as dense regions separated by low-density areas. It doesn't require specifying K in advance. Points in sparse regions are labelled as outliers (label = -1). It handles arbitrary cluster shapes that K-means cannot.

content.code:
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Find good eps using k-NN distance plot
k = 4
nbrs = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k).fit(X_sc)
distances, _ = nbrs.kneighbors(X_sc)
distances = np.sort(distances[:, k-1])  # k-th nearest neighbour distance
# Look for the 'knee' in this plot — that's your eps
plt.plot(distances)
plt.xlabel('Points (sorted)')
plt.ylabel(f'{k}-NN distance')
plt.title('K-NN Distance Plot (find the knee for eps)')
plt.show()

# Fit DBSCAN
db = DBSCAN(eps=0.5, min_samples=5)
labels = db.fit_predict(X_sc)

n_clusters = len(set(labels)) - (1 if -1 in labels else 0)
n_outliers = (labels == -1).sum()
print(f'Found {n_clusters} clusters, {n_outliers} outliers')

content.text: Principal Component Analysis projects high-dimensional data into fewer dimensions while retaining as much variance as possible. Use it for visualisation (reduce to 2D/3D), noise removal, or to speed up downstream models.

content.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Fit PCA
pca = PCA(n_components=0.95)  # keep 95% of variance
X_pca = pca.fit_transform(X_sc)
print(f'Reduced from {X_sc.shape[1]} to {pca.n_components_} components')
print(f'Explained variance ratio: {pca.explained_variance_ratio_.cumsum()[-1]:.3f}')

# Visualise in 2D
pca2d = PCA(n_components=2)
X_2d = pca2d.fit_transform(X_sc)
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.scatter(X_2d[:, 0], X_2d[:, 1], c=labels, cmap='tab10', alpha=0.6, s=10)
plt.xlabel(f'PC1 ({pca2d.explained_variance_ratio_[0]*100:.1f}% variance)')
plt.ylabel(f'PC2 ({pca2d.explained_variance_ratio_[1]*100:.1f}% variance)')
plt.title('PCA Projection')
plt.colorbar(label='Cluster')
plt.show()

a.name: K-Means
a.description: Partition-based — assigns every point to exactly one of K clusters
strengths: Works well for spherical, equal-sized clusters
weaknesses: Assumes spherical clusters of similar size
a.useWhen: You know roughly how many clusters to expect and clusters are roughly spherical

b.name: DBSCAN
b.description: Density-based — groups dense regions, marks sparse points as outliers
weaknesses: Sensitive to eps and min_samples parameters
b.useWhen: You don't know K, clusters have irregular shapes, or outlier detection matters

content.text: Always standardise features before clustering. K-means uses Euclidean distance — features with large numeric ranges will dominate the distance calculation if not scaled.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of DBSCAN over K-means?
options: DBSCAN is always faster than K-means
DBSCAN finds clusters of arbitrary shape and identifies outliers automatically
DBSCAN works better on high-dimensional data
questions.explanation: DBSCAN identifies clusters as dense regions of arbitrary shape and labels sparse points as outliers, unlike K-means which assumes spherical clusters and must assign every point to a cluster.

questions.question: What does the silhouette score measure?
options: How similar each point is to its own cluster compared to other clusters
The total number of clusters found
The percentage of outliers in the dataset
questions.explanation: Silhouette score measures cohesion (similarity within cluster) vs separation (similarity to other clusters). Values near 1.0 indicate well-separated, tight clusters.

questions.question: What is PCA primarily used for in machine learning?
options: Reducing the number of features while retaining most of the variance
Improving precision and recall of classifiers
questions.explanation: PCA reduces dimensionality by projecting data onto the directions of maximum variance (principal components). This compresses data, removes noise, and enables 2D/3D visualisation.

faq.q: How do I evaluate clustering quality without labels?
faq.a: Use the Silhouette Score (how similar a point is to its cluster vs other clusters — values near 1.0 are good) or the Davies-Bouldin Index (lower is better). The Elbow Method uses inertia (within-cluster sum of squares) to suggest a good K.

faq.q: Should I use PCA before clustering?
faq.a: Often yes for high-dimensional data. PCA removes noise dimensions and speeds up K-means. Keep enough components to explain 90-95% of variance (n_components=0.95). Don't use PCA if the number of features is small (< 20).

faq.q: What is the difference between PCA and t-SNE?
faq.a: PCA is a linear transform that preserves global variance — it's fast and reproducible. t-SNE is a non-linear transform that preserves local neighbourhood structure — it's better for visualisation but very slow on large datasets and results depend on the perplexity parameter.
